catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achille-gagli:
Achille Gagliardi was a Paduan ascetic writer and spiritual director, born in 1537, who died at Modena on 6 July 1607. His brilliant Padua University career preceded his 1559 entry into the Society of Jesus with two younger brothers. He taught philosophy at the Roman College and theology at Padua and Milan, and ran several northern Italian houses of his order with success.

He preached, gave retreats, and directed congregations with tireless zeal, and St. Charles Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, held him in great esteem as theologian and guide. Borromeo took him on pastoral visitations and asked him to publish his popular handbook, Catechismo della fede cattolica, in 1584. His Breve compendio on Christian perfection, printed after his death, was translated into five languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnolo-giovan:
Agnolo, Giovanni, and Taddeo Gaddi were Florentine artists. Taddeo was father of Agnolo and Giovanni. Their birth dates are very uncertain: Taddeo probably about 1300, his sons after 1333. Giovanni died in 1383, Agnolo in 1396, the father in 1366. All three lie buried in Florence's Santa Croce. Taddeo was Giotto's godson, spent twenty-four years with him, becoming the most eminent of his many scholars.

Vasari says Taddeo surpassed his master in colour and sometimes in expression. Two signed paintings survive: one in Berlin dated 1333, one at Mogognano dated 1355. His best extant frescoes are in Santa Croce's Giugni Chapel. He is perhaps best known as architect of Florence's Ponte Vecchio and the finer Ponte Trinita downstream, destroyed in the sixteenth century. His son Agnolo's best work is at Prato cathedral and Santa Croce, and he taught Cennino Cennini, whose treatise is the chief source on early Florentine technique.

erewhon-revisited-twenty-years-later-bot:
Samuel Butler returned to his upside-down country in Erewhon Revisited, published in 1901, twenty years after the original discoverer's escape. His preface asks what followed when Higgs ascended in a balloon with Arowhena before the Erewhonians' eyes: a miracle demanding a religion. The answer fills the sequel, told partly by Higgs's son.

The younger Higgs travels into Erewhon and finds his father worshipped as the Sunchild, with professors Hanky and Panky guarding the new faith's evidence and quarreling over nuggets in a hollow tree. Butler aims at the founding of Christianity by parody, and at his own earlier book. The satire is gentler and sadder than Erewhon, and its target, respectable belief, has lost none of its polish.
first-across-the-continent-the-story-of-:
Noah Brooks retold the Lewis and Clark expedition in First Across the Continent, covering the exploring years 1804 to 1806. His first chapter, A Great Transaction in Land, begins with America's astonishment at Napoleon's sale of Louisiana for fifteen million dollars, arranged by Livingston and Monroe with Barbe-Marbois. Jefferson's explorers then set out to learn what the nation had bought.

Brooks follows the journals closely: rivers, hailstorms that drop rain and snow within miles of each other, capsized canoes, and merchandise dried slowly after soakings. Sacagawea, the Mandan winter, and the Pacific arrival all appear in journal language. Written for general readers, the book keeps the expedition's daily texture while making its national meaning plain.
govdocs-archive_org-meditations-on-the-p:
Julius Evola climbed mountains as a young man, and in Meditations on the Peaks he treats the high ranges as more than sport. For Evola the mountain is a symbol of spiritual ascent, and climbing becomes a discipline of the inner life.

The essays set out his doctrine of the mountain: height as purity, effort as initiation, the summit as a meeting with the sacred. He writes against turning mountaineering into tourism or athletics alone. The book gathers his mountain writings into one of his most personal works, where landscape and metaphysics are treated as the same subject.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: Cheddi Jagan, the elected leader of British Guiana, was driven from office in 1964 after a campaign of pressure in which the CIA played a covert part. This briefing-book page presents the record of those operations in the small South American colony. The evidence here is the title alone, so the specific documents cannot be named. The case matters beyond its size: it showed Washington applying Cold War covert methods in the Caribbean basin, against a leftist who had won at the ballot box.
heidi:
Johanna Spyri wrote Heidi, the story of a Swiss orphan girl sent to live with her grandfather, Alm-Uncle, in a hut above an Alpine village. Heidi thrives among goats, hay beds, and mountain air, visiting the blind grandmother of goatherd Peter. Then a housekeeper's plan takes her to Frankfurt as companion to Clara Sesemann, a girl who cannot walk.

In the great house Heidi sickens with homesickness and walks in her sleep, taken for a ghost. Sent home, she recovers, learns to read, and softens her grandfather's hard heart. Clara's later visit to the mountain brings the famous ending. Spyri wrote for children and for those who love children, as her title page said.
john-thorndyke-s-cases-related-by-christ:
John Thorndyke's Cases is a set of detective stories by R. Austin Freeman, told by Christopher Jervis. Thorndyke is a doctor-detective whose cases turn on exact physical evidence. Eight cases fill the book, from The Man with the Nailed Shoes to A Message from the Deep Sea. Photographs and drawings of clues appear throughout the volume.

The cases include a stranger's latchkey, a blue sequin, a Moabite cipher, and a mandarin's pearl. An aluminium dagger and an anthropologist at large round out the set. The picture list shows hair sections, sand from a pillow, and a sergeant's sketch. Freeman built these tales on careful forensic method, clue by clue.
nasa-tm-19640019268-the-electrical-chara: Goddard Space Flight Center issued this study on March 30, 1964. It treats the electrical traits of silicon solar cells that have been exposed to radiation. How those traits shift with temperature is the report's stated focus. Solar cells power most satellites, and space radiation slowly harms them. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable abstract or body text, so its data cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660020186-extraterrestrial-app:
H K Herglotz presented this study at a Marshall space science seminar in February 1966, issued on April 20, 1966. X-ray diffraction can name the elements in a sample and identify many compounds and minerals. Herglotz calls it a promising candidate for exploring the surfaces of the Moon and of Earth-like planets. That promise holds only if gear fit for space can be built, he adds.

He describes the method's fundamentals first. Then he turns to the difficulties of using it off Earth. Weight, power, and handling samples without human hands all stand in the way. Later lunar and Mars landers did carry such instruments, along the path this paper surveyed.
nasa-tm-19670022936-flight-test-of-a-31-:
John S. Preisser, Clinton V. Eckstrom, and Harold N. Murrow, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, flight-tested a parachute in this report. The canopy was a modified ringsail, about thirty-one feet across. It deployed above the speed of sound, under the NASA Planetary Entry Parachute Program.

A mortar fired the parachute out behind an instrumented payload at Mach 1.39. The canopy reached line stretch in a fraction of a second, then inflated quickly to full open. The peak opening load came just as the canopy filled. The test proved a big ringsail could open safely at supersonic speed and very low air pressure.
nasa-tm-19680013268-viewing-devices-for-:
Lawrence A. Mueller and David W. Medwid of NASA's Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 memorandum on windows for hot mercury systems. Space power units that boil and condense liquid metals need a clear way to watch the flow inside. The authors studied windows for a mercury condensing tube and a mercury boiler outlet tube.

Matching how the window, sealants, and support expand with heat proved central to the design. The condensing tube window was tested with flowing mercury at high heat and pressure, then shaken at room temperature. The boiler window was heated in a furnace under gas pressure. Sealants, window shapes, and metal to glass joints were all checked under harsh test conditions.
nasa-tm-19680028473-melting-relationship:
A. F. Koster van Groos, a resident research associate at Goddard Space Flight Center, and P. J. Wyllie, of the University of Chicago, studied melting in a rock-like chemical system under pressure. Their mixture joins a sodium aluminum silicon oxide with salt and water, squeezed at one kilobar. Such systems help geologists read how real magmas melt and crystallize deep underground.

Chapters describe the starting materials, the pressure apparatus, and how each mineral phase was identified. Results follow for the dry salt mixture and for the mixture with water added. A long discussion traces courses of crystallization and the effect of pressure itself. The report closes with petrological applications, tying the laboratory melts to natural rocks.
nasa-tm-19690029214-experimental-investi:
James E. Calogeras of Lewis Research Center investigated dynamic distortion in a supersonic inlet in this October 1969 memorandum. Tests ran in the Lewis 10-by-10-Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel at Mach 2.50. The inlet had sixty percent internal contraction and fed a J85-GE-13 turbojet engine.

Average pressure fluctuations of only a small share of total pressure could completely degrade stall margin at certain engine speeds, he found. Vortex generators suppressed dynamic distortion at off-design conditions much better than throat bleed did. The engine's presence changed neither the size nor the spread of the distortion. Inlet-engine compatibility work like this protects engines from sudden stalls in supersonic flight.
nasa-tm-19700009496-flight-control-of-th:
M. P. Frank of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this paper in December 1969. He had presented it in Tokyo in August that year. It explains how flight controllers in Houston ran the Apollo lunar landing mission.

Frank first describes the worldwide tracking and data network that fed the control center. He then covers the center itself and how it passed spacecraft and crew data to the flight control team. The paper lays out how the control team was organized and which skills it drew on. It ends with a detailed account of the flight control work during a landing mission.
nasa-tm-19710008389-motor-starting-chara:
David S. Repas and Robert J. Frye of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in March 1971. It records how a modified Lundell alternator behaves when it starts as a motor. The machine was designed for a single-shaft Brayton-cycle space power system.

To start the whole power loop, the alternator itself must spin up first. The team started it as an induction motor and measured the run. They logged armature current, shaft speed, and field voltage through the start. Torque was then figured from the measured speeding-up and the rotor's inertia. A power system that cannot start itself is dead weight in orbit.
notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-2-may-:
Volume two of Notes and Queries ran from May to December 1850, and this file holds its index. The journal served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, per its title page. Its motto stayed Captain Cuttle's rule: when found, make a note of. Entries point by page to notes, queries, and replies.

Under A, a note treats the solemnization of matrimony, and many pages treat aerostation, or balloon flight. The Agapemone, Agincourt, and a cure for ague by spiders all appear. Ale draper gets a meaning hunt, and Alfred's Orosius a note. Apricot and peach etymology closes the sampled run. No topic was too small for its pages.
on-the-method-of-zadig-essay-1-from-scie:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this essay on scientific method. It is essay one from Science and Hebrew Tradition. His subtitle calls it retrospective prophecy in science. Zadig is a figure from a tale by Voltaire. Cuvier had praised Zadig's sure marks of reasoning.

Zadig retired to the banks of the Euphrates River. Patient study of plants and animals sharpened his sight. He learned to spot minute differences in similar things. Huxley uses him to show how science reasons backward. Small clues reveal past events, as tracks reveal animals. He lived, the tale says, at Babylon under King Moabdar. No king list since found names that king at all.
podcast-dannyjones-5_vzzUlAoDI:
Fraudster Matthew Cox returns for KONCRETE number 46 with Danny Jones. Fans keep asking for Cox back on the show. This visit is billed as a look inside a pathological liar's mind.

Cox has served time for huge mortgage fraud schemes. He now tells his story as both warning and show. Jones asks how lying became habit, craft, and income. Cox brings props and treats the talk like a stage act. The episode lets a proud con man explain his own thinking, which makes it both gripping and hard to fully trust.
podcast-joerogan-8xRz8ra9mdI:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1530 of the Joe Rogan Experience finds the comedian in his familiar role: half jester, half seeker. Trussell had by then become one of the show's defining guests, known for turning any topic into a trip through myth and mind.

The conversation floats across psychedelics, the self, and the strange comfort of not knowing. Rogan grounds the riffs with stories from his own life and work. Longtime listeners will hear the pair's rhythm at its smoothest here, while new listeners get a fair sample of why Trussell's visits are treated as events by the show's fans.
report-of-mr-w-e-cormack-s-journey-in-se:
W. E. Cormack read this report of his journey in search of the Red Indians of Newfoundland before the Boeothick Institution at St. John's. The meeting was held on January 12, 1828, with A. W. Desbarres in the chair. The Institution had been formed to open contact with the Red Indians and to record their history.

Cormack, the Institution's president, outlines his expedition rather than giving its full detail. His party held three men besides himself: an able Abenakie man from Canada, an elder Mountaineer from Labrador, and a young Micmack native of the island. They had meant to start at White Bay and travel south, but weather blocked the plan.
targum-or-metrical-translations-from-thi:
George Borrow made Targum, a set of verse renderings drawn from thirty tongues and dialects, picked from a vast heap of work built up over years of language study. Borrow offers the pieces with frank doubt about his own success in spots.

He argues that the hardest part of verse rendering is not the words but the cast and turn of the source. He praises Fairfax, who put Tasso's Jerusalem into English octave rhyme, as a rare master of that art. Borrow also holds that a nation's tone shows best in its songs, from soft Persian airs to bold Danish war ditties. Readers get a wide, odd tour of world song.
the-kasi-dah-of-ha-ji-abdu-el-yezdi:
The Kasîdah of Hâjî Abdû El-Yezdî calls itself a lay of the higher law. The author's friend and pupil F. B. translated and annotated it. A note to the reader is signed from Vienna. November 1880 is its date. The note lays out the poem's principles. Happiness and misery are equally divided in the world. Self-cultivation, with due regard to others, is life's sole object. The affections and the gift of pity are man's highest joys. Judgment should be suspended, the note adds. Facts deserve proper suspicion.

The poem opens at nightfall. The waning moon walks forth to rule the later night. A star's sparkle crowns it. F. B. concedes the work looks destructive. It is essentially reconstructive, he says. Curious readers are sent to the volume's end for details. Richard Burton's poem wears a Persian mask here. It asks to be read as wisdom, not narrative.
the-method-by-which-the-causes-of-the-pr:
Thomas H. Huxley's lecture on the method for discovering the causes of the present and past condition of organic nature was delivered to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863. It forms the third of six lectures on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley recaps two earlier lectures on the extent of the subject. He then turns to the great problem: what knowledge we have of the causes behind organic phenomena.

An objection meets him at the threshold, from worthy people who hold that vital phenomena lie outside ordinary inquiry. Such objectors call the origin of life miraculous and further questions presumptuous. Huxley answers with the story of Diogenes, who refuted a sophist's proof that motion was impossible by simply getting up and walking. Science, he says, replies the same way, by pointing to the immense mass of facts already systematized under morphology, development, and distribution.
